stories.headline: SpaceX catches Ship 42 with the tower arms after 22.5 hours in orbit, the first orbital upper stage ever brought home
stories.why_read: Your last night on X was almost nothing but this catch, and it deserves the top slot: full reusability just stopped being a slide and became a video.
body: SpaceX closed out Starship Flight 15 on Saturday by catching Ship 42 in the Mechazilla tower's chopsticks at Starbase, roughly 22.5 hours after liftoff, according to a summary of posts on X. The ship had reached orbit on November 13, deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and circled Earth before coming home. Commentator Dan Huot called it the Holy Grail of spaceflight, and posts you reposted note that Starship is now the largest object ever to go to orbit and be recovered.

Not everything went to plan: Super Heavy splashed down in the Gulf instead of being caught, and one engineering account you reposted says the booster simply ran short of propellant. Still, the reactions say a lot. Walter Isaacson recalled engineers' faces in December 2020 when Elon Musk insisted the tower arms could catch a returning ship, and Demis Hassabis called the sonic thunderclap before the catch one of the coolest things he has ever seen.

stories.headline: Inside SpaceXAI's Grok Bot team: agents as teammates, 11,000 pull requests in a month and a 0.5% rollback rate
stories.why_read: You run a whole fleet of these bots, so this is the rare behind-the-scenes look at how the people building them actually work, from lint rules to Slack-thread shipping.
body: Engineers at SpaceXAI described building Grok Bot, where AI agents run on their own cloud computers with browsers, files and terminals, sign into apps, and pass work between each other, according to a summary of posts on X. Lauren Tan (@poteto) shared that her small team hit about 11,000 pull requests in a month with roughly 0.5% rollbacks, treating agents as coworkers that take code from start to finish. The product went from start to launch in seven weeks.

The interesting part for an architect is the guardrails: strict architecture, lint rules, and self-verification so agents can ship without a human babysitting every diff. A companion thread shows heavy users wiring up Chief of Staff style bots that book FedEx pickups and run CRMs, with some running dozens of agents on the Ultra plan. Usage spikes have strained limits along the way.

stories.headline: Forensics on published weights suggest DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant trained new models on export-controlled Blackwell GPUs
stories.why_read: Export controls usually get argued with leaks and anonymous sources; this one argues from the numbers inside the open weights themselves, which is a much more interesting kind of evidence.
body: A report by Will DePue at Unemployment Labs says six models released since April 2026 by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry numerical patterns that match Nvidia's Blackwell hardware, while earlier models from the same labs match the older Hopper generation. The team recovers traces of the models' initial values and searches for hardware configurations that reproduce them, and says it confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3.

The authors are careful to say the fingerprint shows how the weights were created and supports, without proving, that Blackwell also did the training. They rule out specially configured AMD hardware for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and call it very unlikely for the rest. It landed on Hacker News near the top of the week's AI threads, and it adds a technical layer to a policy fight that has mostly run on accusations.

stories.headline: Google Project Zero drops its 30-day patch soak and will disclose bugs 90 days after reporting, citing AI-speed exploitation
stories.why_read: If you own patch pipelines at work, this is the policy change that resets everyone's clock: Project Zero now treats patch-to-exploit time as roughly zero.
body: Since 2021 Project Zero followed a 90 plus 30 policy: vendors got 90 days to fix a bug plus 30 days of soak time for rollout. The team now says AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation make that timeline clearly insufficient. LLMs let attackers find bugs faster, raise the odds that several parties find the same bug, and can reverse engineer a patch almost immediately, so the extra soak time mainly creates a false sense of secrecy.

The post also says LLMs have raised the volume of bugs Project Zero itself reports, to several a week in some targets. It pushes vendors to shrink the patch gap, the time between a fix shipping and users installing it, either by rolling out faster or by protecting users while remediation is still underway. Expect other disclosure programs to be asked why they still allow longer windows.

stories.headline: Michael Dell: H100 rental prices rose from $1.96 to $3.10 an hour in a year, on a chip that first shipped in 2022
stories.why_read: You reposted this one, and it is the cleanest single data point on how tight inference compute still is: old GPUs are getting more expensive, not cheaper.
body: Michael Dell posted that Dell started shipping Nvidia's H100 in 2022, that a year ago it rented for $1.96 per hour, and that today it rents for $3.10, a 58% increase. Normally a three-year-old accelerator would be sliding down the price curve as newer parts arrive. Instead, demand for inference and training capacity is keeping even previous-generation hardware fully booked.

The number sits alongside other signals from this week: Saturday's edition covered WSJ reporting on Nvidia helping small clouds buy its GPUs, and a DRAM conspiracy suit (below) argues memory makers shifted capacity toward HBM. For anyone planning on-prem versus cloud GPU spend, the takeaway is that used and older capacity is not a bargain bin right now.

stories.headline: More than 50 production Cybercabs, some with Starlink antennas, show up in a Dallas lot ahead of robotaxi rides
stories.why_read: After Saturday's Cybercab order news, this is the physical proof: a lot full of steering-wheel-free two-seaters a few hours up I-35 from you.
body: Videos shared on X show dozens of officially badged gold Cybercabs parked in a Dallas lot, with some appearing to carry integrated Starlink hardware, according to a summary of posts. The sightings follow Tesla VP Ashok Elluswamy's October statement that rides would start in Dallas in November, where Model Y robotaxis already run unsupervised. Tesla has not announced a public Cybercab launch date there yet.

Your bookmarks from Friday night were full of the economics behind it. One post you saved compares a full-time chauffeur at roughly $38 an hour with a $300 a month autonomy subscription, which works out to about 40 cents an hour if used around the clock. Another argues that robotaxis in several cities plus Cybercab sales to the public is hard to square with the bear case.

stories.headline: SpaceX and Tesla merger talks advance, with special committees negotiating and an announcement possible by December
stories.why_read: Two of your three favorite companies on X might become one, and the catch this weekend only adds fuel to the valuation talk.
body: Talks between SpaceX and Tesla on a combination are moving forward, with special committees of independent directors negotiating terms, according to summaries of posts on X. Reports put a possible announcement as early as December or in early 2027, and describe a combined company worth roughly $3.4 to $3.5 trillion that would be among the largest in the S&P 500. Prediction markets cited in the coverage put the odds at 91% by the end of 2027.

The obstacles are real: Tesla's China operations, SpaceX's defense contracts, and regulatory approvals all came up. The bull case is synergy across robotics, AI, energy, Starlink and launch. One bookmark you saved makes the de-risking argument directly, saying the leap from expendable to reusable rockets was a harder problem than building satellites that send compute back to Earth.

stories.headline: Researchers scan 159,041 Lovable projects and find personal data, including passports and private messages, readable without login
stories.why_read: This is the security bill for no-code AI app builders coming due, and it is a useful reference the next time someone at work wants to ship a vibe-coded internal tool.
body: German security firm Crissy Field examined 159,041 projects built on Lovable, the Stockholm AI app builder, and reports many cases where personal and confidential information was reachable without logging in. The Hacker News headline summarizing the work says exposed data included passport details and more than 200,000 private messages. The report notes that Lovable's terms place responsibility for application security and data handling on customers.

The researchers' point is the gap between marketing that says no technical knowledge is needed and the reality that access control is still the builder's job. With Lovable generating full apps backed by databases, a missing row-level policy is one prompt away. It is a strong argument for security review and default-deny data access in any agent-built app.

stories.headline: The catch math: about $1 million in propellant for 100 tons to orbit, and ARK sees roughly $100 per kilogram
stories.why_read: Once the cheering stops, this is the part that changes industries, and a few of the posts you saved put real numbers on it.
body: Several posts you bookmarked tried to price what a recovered ship means. One notes that fueling Starship costs about $1 million, so if both the ship and booster come back, propellant becomes the main cost of putting about 100 tons into orbit. A post from ARK's @wintonARK goes further, saying the catch could drop cost per kilogram to orbit to roughly $100 from about $1,000.

Those are estimates, not SpaceX figures, and the booster still was not recovered on this flight. But the direction is clear, and other posts connect it to orbital data centers, military logistics and much cheaper upmass for Starlink. Treat the numbers as a framework for where launch pricing could go if reuse becomes routine.

stories.headline: Rocket Lab flies its 100th Electron, deploying a Japanese radar satellite for iQPS
stories.why_read: A post you saved put it best: Rocket Lab hit 100 launches the same week SpaceX caught Starship, and the two keep running circles around everyone else.
body: Rocket Lab launched its 100th Electron on November 14 from the Māhia Peninsula in New Zealand, placing the YAMATSUMI-II radar satellite for Japan's iQPS into a 575 km orbit, according to a summary of posts on X. The mission flew under a special black-and-gold livery and kept a perfect record on all 11 iQPS flights since 2023.

CEO Peter Beck credited innovations like 3D-printed engines and said the company is building a rocket roughly every eight days, with more than 100 launches booked. Ashlee Vance captured the mood on your timeline: Rocket Lab doing 100 rockets and SpaceX catching Starship in the same week shows how far ahead these two are.

stories.headline: Why SpaceX turned three of Starship's satellites into cameras
stories.why_read: You reposted Farzad's explainer, and it is the right companion to the catch footage: it answers why we got such good views of the ship this time.
body: Farzad's video explainer looks at why SpaceX used three of the satellites on Starship's flight as camera platforms rather than pure payload. Watching a ship in orbit, deploying satellites and preparing for reentry is hard to capture from the ground or from onboard cameras alone, and dedicated imaging gives engineers and the public a view of the vehicle from outside.

It is a short watch, and it pairs well with the posts you reposted about Starlink V3 capacity and the ship's 14 orbits before coming home. If you want the why behind the imagery that filled your timeline this weekend, start here.

stories.headline: Claude Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5 or the free Gemini 4 Hydrogen? Developers argue over which model to code with
stories.why_read: You reposted Peter Yang saying Claude is his daily driver again, and this thread is the broader version of that choice, with prices attached.
body: Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12 as a fast model with a free tier and paid pricing of $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, according to a summary of posts on X. Developers are stacking it against Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2, released November 9 with a one-million-token context, and Opus 5.5, which costs about half as much as Fable.

The emerging consensus is a split: Fable edges ahead on long agentic coding runs, many people keep Opus as the reliable daily driver, and Hydrogen is the budget option for quick iteration. Peter Yang's new tutorial, which you reposted, walks through which model he uses for which kind of real work, which is a practical way to set your own defaults.

stories.headline: Google Research shows Antigravity's /teamwork agents working on open problems in math, chemistry and kernel optimization
stories.why_read: After Saturday's Dynamic Workflows story, this is Google's multi-agent pitch aimed at real research, and the tools are being opened to outside researchers.
body: In a November 13 Google Research post, Vahab Mirrokni describes teams across Google and academic partners using Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen with Antigravity's /teamwork multi-agent workflows on long-open problems. He cites new results in information theory, formal verification, molecular structure discovery and kernel optimization, plus several production infrastructure gains at Google.

The framing is a discovery loop: humans set the questions and the physical or theoretical constraints, while long-horizon agents write custom solvers, search large spaces and test candidates. Google says it is making these agents available in Antigravity's /teamwork, alongside /boost, and through a researcher access program.

stories.headline: Obsidian ships Obsidian Skills, teaching agents to fully operate your vaults and wikis
stories.why_read: You reposted this from kepano, and it is aimed squarely at your setup: a vault plus a fleet of bots that file notes into it.
body: Obsidian CEO Steph Ango (@kepano) announced Obsidian Skills, described as a way to teach your agents how to fully operate your vaults and wikis. Skills are packaged instructions that coding and personal agents load on demand, so an official set from Obsidian means agents can learn the app's conventions directly instead of guessing at file formats and links.

For anyone already running agents that write into a vault, this could replace hand-rolled prompts with a maintained, official playbook. It is worth comparing against whatever conventions your own note-filing bots follow today.

stories.headline: Judge refuses to dismiss suit accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of starving DDR5 supply to favor HBM
stories.why_read: If you have wondered why server memory got so expensive, this case puts that exact theory in front of a federal judge.
body: U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California on November 14 denied in full a joint motion by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to dismiss a proposed class action, LitNews reports. The suit alleges the three conspired to cut supply of conventional DRAM such as DDR5 and shift capacity to HBM for AI accelerators. The judge held it was not a rerun of an earlier DRAM conspiracy case the Ninth Circuit dismissed in 2022.

The court pointed to long-term HBM lock-ups, refusals of long-term conventional DRAM contracts, Micron's Crucial closure, fab delays and the companies' cartel history as supporting a plausible inference of conspiracy. It gave no weight to investor talk of supply discipline or to conference meetings. Answers are due December 7, with a case management conference reset to January 12, 2027.

stories.headline: Microsoft's FORGE Lab uses an AI scanner to find memory safety bugs in Rust's standard library, some reachable from safe code
stories.why_read: This pairs neatly with the Project Zero story: AI-driven bug hunting is now finding flaws even in the foundations people trust most.
body: Microsoft's FORGE Lab reports several memory safety issues in Rust's std and core libraries, including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The work used Hyenas, a research version of an AI vulnerability scanning system code-named MDASH. The team includes people behind Rudra, an earlier static analyzer for unsafe Rust.

The findings fall into three patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. With Microsoft, GitHub, Android, Linux and Cloudflare all moving code to Rust, the post argues that bugs in the foundational libraries carry outsized consequences.

stories.headline: Kiri, a Rust container runtime, claims 22 ms docker run versus 178 ms on Docker Desktop, with the Docker CLI and Compose intact
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this one, and it is worth a test drive on your Mac: a drop-in Docker Desktop alternative that keeps your existing commands.
body: Kiri bills itself as a modern container runtime that runs Docker containers with one daemon, while the docker CLI, Compose and the Docker Engine API work as they do today. Its own benchmark says docker run takes 22 ms on Kiri versus 178 ms on Docker Desktop, 152 ms on Colima and 279 ms on OrbStack, with every engine on 2 CPUs and 8 GB.

Version 0.2.1 is free and in beta on Mac, Windows and Linux, and the bookmark you saved describes it as tiny and written in Rust. The speed numbers are the vendor's own, so they deserve a local check, but low overhead plus Compose compatibility is exactly what makes a runtime easy to swap in.

stories.headline: DeepSeek V3's architecture in 190 lines of pure JAX, pretrained from scratch on a MacBook Air
stories.why_read: If you want to actually understand MLA and DeepSeekMoE rather than nod along, this is the most readable implementation you will find this week.
body: Vaibhaav Tiwari's repository implements the architecture from the DeepSeek-V3 technical report in about 190 lines of pure JAX, with no Flax, Equinox or PyTorch. It covers Multi-head Latent Attention, DeepSeekMoE, auxiliary-loss-free load balancing and multi-token prediction, and keeps parameters as plain dictionaries of arrays so every piece reads top to bottom.

The model was pretrained from scratch on a MacBook Air using public-domain detective fiction, and a companion write-up explains the code piece by piece with diagrams. In this toy setup, MLA caches 144 numbers per token per layer instead of 480. It drew a big Show HN response.

stories.headline: PyPI's redesigned project pages go live with a security tab showing provenance and per-file attestations
stories.why_read: Supply-chain signals only help if people can read them, and PyPI just made them visible on every package page you check.
body: The Python Package Index finished the interface updates it announced in July. The redesign, shaped by user research and built with Kabu Creative, adds a security tab that explains release provenance and shows per-file digital attestations, following the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide.

PyPI says the ecosystem's growth has made it a bigger target for malicious packages, and attestations, introduced in 2024, give a verifiable record of where a release file came from. Until now the site did little to explain what that meant. Release files and history also got clearer layouts.

stories.headline: tsoracle: an embeddable Rust timestamp oracle for strictly monotonic timestamps and gapless sequences
stories.why_read: This is the Spanner and CockroachDB trick packaged as a small service, plus gapless IDs for invoices and ledgers, which is a very architect-shaped tool.
body: tsoracle is a distributed, fault-tolerant timestamp oracle written in Rust. A TSO hands out strictly increasing IDs that order events across machines, which you need for MVCC databases, merging change data across shards and audit logs. The project notes that Spanner, CockroachDB and FoundationDB all rely on the same idea internally.

Its twist is gapless sequences: get_seq() returns contiguous numbers per named key, with nothing skipped or reused across crashes or failover, which suits invoice numbers and ledger lines. Window state is fsync'd before any timestamp is issued, and consensus is pluggable, with openraft in production.

stories.headline: Tesla buys its first Times Square billboard to advertise Full Self-Driving
stories.why_read: Tesla famously does not advertise, so a billboard in the middle of Manhattan says a lot about how hard it is now pushing FSD adoption.
body: Tesla has placed its first billboard in Times Square to promote Full Self-Driving, according to a summary of posts on X. The ad claims FSD is 7 times safer than human drivers, based on Tesla's own data, and cites more than 15 billion miles driven globally. It runs through November on a screen owned by JPMorgan Chase.

Fans read it as a shift away from Tesla's long reliance on word of mouth, coming as FSD usage rises and regulators keep watching the supervised system. Combined with Cybercab orders and the Dallas fleet, it rounds out a week of Tesla going on offense about autonomy.

stories.headline: Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth on November 18
stories.why_read: A gentle reminder that a 1977 spacecraft is still talking to us, and NASA is inviting everyone to wave back with a flashlight.
body: On November 18 at 5:16 a.m. Eastern, Voyager 1 will reach one full light-day from Earth, more than 16 billion miles away, according to a summary of posts on X. Launched in 1977, it has been in interstellar space since 2012 and still sends data on cosmic rays and magnetic fields, with engineers shutting down instruments over time to stretch its fading power.

NASA is asking people to celebrate after sunset on November 17 by flashing VGR in Morse code toward the sky with a flashlight or phone. It is a nice family activity for Tuesday evening, and a good companion to a weekend of reusable rockets.

stories.headline: Quanta: a new generation of scientists rethinks how chemistry turned into biology
stories.why_read: This fits the physics and chemistry corner of your pinned post: a long, careful read on the oldest open question in science.
body: Quanta's Yasemin Saplakoglu reports that after decades of arguing over which molecules came first, researchers are rethinking what life was, is and could be. The story is part of an Origins of Life week package focused on the roughly 200 million years after conditions for life emerged on Earth but before our most ancient single-celled ancestor appeared.

It walks from Earth's molten, meteorite-battered early days to acidic oceans under carbon dioxide skies, then into the competing ideas about metabolism, RNA and cells. A good weekend read that rewards slow attention.

stories.headline: Oxford's molecular motors group explains the bacterial flagellar motor, a 45-nanometer rotary engine
stories.why_read: Engineering is magic, as one post in your bookmarks put it, and nature built this rotary motor long before we built any.
body: Oxford Physics' Molecular Motors group describes the bacterial flagellar motor, a rotary engine powered by ions flowing across the cell membrane. Each motor drives a helical filament that spins at hundreds of revolutions per second to make the cell swim. The rotor is a set of rings about 45 nm across made of a few hundred protein molecules.

Around it sit independent torque generators built from the proteins MotA and MotB, with room for at least 11 in E. coli. Structures from 2020 suggest a MotA5 MotB2 complex where the five-part ring turns around the pair, coupled to proton flow, like little wheels. It is a lovely blend of physics and biology.

stories.headline: A family tree of 104 software job titles, from human 'Computer' to 'AI Agent / Context Engineer'
stories.why_read: As an IT architect who has watched DevOps become SRE become platform engineering, you will enjoy finding your own branch on this tree.
body: Ian Miell, a former Head of DevOps, built a family tree of software job titles from the 1940s to now with help from Claude. It covers 104 titles in seven families, including development, architecture and leadership, operations and infrastructure, networks and security, and data and AI, with time running top to bottom in five-year rows.

Solid arrows mean a title grew out of its parent and dashed arrows mean influence or a common career move. The whole thing is one Graphviz file and one JSON file of descriptions, and clicking a title shows its history. The dates are his estimates of when titles became common, not first use.

stories.headline: Why buy a Raspberry Pi when an old phone already has the camera, GPS, battery and modem?
stories.why_read: A fun, practical homelab read: the parts math makes a strong case for the drawer of retired phones most of us have.
body: The author needs a high-resolution camera, GPS, storage and a microcontroller for a lighting project, and compares a Raspberry Pi build with used phones like a Redmi 13C 5G and Huawei Mate 30 5G. Those phones sell second hand for about ¥300 to ¥500, roughly $45 to $75, and already include a 50MP or 40MP camera, GPS, storage, clock, battery, touchscreen and mobile data.

By the author's tally, a Pi 4 core build with camera, GPS hat and storage runs about ¥1,483, and a fully equipped one with RTC, UPS, display and 4G is around ¥2,317. The rooted phone talks to an LED controller board over USB-C. It is a good reminder that e-waste can be a dev board.

stories.headline: A simple trick: Tailscale on laptop and phone, then have Claude Code or Codex send you a preview link you can open anywhere
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this tip, and it is a nice fit with the Tailscale-heavy homelab setup you already run.
body: A post you saved lays out a quick workflow: install Tailscale on your computer and phone on the same free account, open a project in Claude Code or Codex, and ask the agent to run the project and send you a preview link. Because both devices sit on the same tailnet, the link opens on your phone without exposing anything to the public internet.

It is a small idea, but it turns a coding agent into something you can check from the couch or the airport. Pair it with the Grok Bot team story above and you can see where agent workflows are heading: start work in one place and review it from anywhere.

stories.headline: SpaceX donates Starlink kits to childcare centers in 16 countries, including 210 in Nigeria
stories.why_read: For the love and kindness part of your pinned post: connectivity used to help reunite families and protect kids.
body: SpaceX handed Starlink kits to the Lagos State Ministry of Youth and Social Development as part of a grant of 750 units for childcare institutions in 16 countries, 210 of them in Nigeria, according to a summary of posts on X. Each kit includes up to 12 months of free service to support digital record keeping, staff training, family reunification and child protection.
The donation is being delivered through the nonprofit Both Ends Believing, with most units rolling out by early 2027. It is a quiet counterpoint to a loud weekend of rocket news.

stories.headline: A job application asks AIs to name their favorite ML concept and humans their favorite snack; 27 applicants admitted they were AI
stories.why_read: A genuinely funny story with a real lesson about AI-written applications, the kind of thing you would forward to a hiring manager.
body: Pangram Labs added a question to its job applications: if you are an AI, name your favorite machine learning concept, otherwise share your favorite snack. In one month, 27 applicants said they were AI, 1,217 named ML concepts, and more than 1,000 gave vague or repeated answers like trail mix, according to a summary of posts on X.
Co-founder Max Spero said the question cut review time by 60%. It is a clever, low-tech filter, and a reminder of how many applications are now outsourced to bots end to end.

stories.headline: Lauren Tan's lesson of the year: don't ask whether you should do the thing; do it, then come back with a demo
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this, and it is the human side of the lead story: the same person behind those 11,000 PRs on how she follows through.
body: Lauren Tan (@poteto) wrote that the lesson she learned this year helped her follow through on ideas instead of getting stuck overthinking them: don't ask if you should do the thing, do it, then come back with a demo or something tangible. You can just do things.

It is short, but it lands differently coming from someone whose team runs agents as teammates. When building is this cheap, a working demo beats a proposal, and that applies to architecture reviews as much as side projects.
